story: You arrived at the Moon's south pole on an Artemis lander. The Sun circles low in the sky here, and some craters never see daylight.
Your crew is working far from the outpost. Until they return, the outpost is yours to run: power, air, water and food.
Keep everything alive, collect samples, and survive solar storms for 32 days. Then the crew lander will come to take you home.
ending_success: The crew lander touches down. You kept the outpost alive for 32 days. Well done, astronaut!
Real missions need exactly this: careful power, clean air, enough water and food, and a safe place when the Sun gets angry.
ending_failed: This mission did not work out, but every astronaut learns from practice.
Check your power, air, water and food, and run to the shelter when a storm comes. Try again, you can do it!
credits: Space weather data: NASA CCMC DONKI (archive downloaded from the CCMC host). The 2003 flare: NOAA / ESA.
NASA OSDR (study OSD-804), RadLab / ISS DOSIS 3D-DOSTEL dosimetry, Canadian Space Agency food production toolkit.
Research sources: see the repository README.

Code: written with AI assistance (Claude Code by Anthropic) and tested and adjusted by the team during the event.
Font: Pixelify Sans by Stefie Justprince, SIL Open Font License 1.1 (Google Fonts).
Sound effects: made with jsfxr (and Audacity if used) during the event.
This game is not endorsed by NASA.

welcome.title: Welcome to the south pole
welcome.body: The Sun circles low here, so there is no daily night. But some craters are always dark, and the Moon's shadows can block the Sun for days.

breathing.title: Breathing
breathing.body: One astronaut breathes about 0.84 kg of oxygen every day. Your habitat keeps a reserve of oxygen, and life support keeps it topped up.

radishes.title: Radishes
radishes.body: Radishes grow fast. On the Space Station plants take about 27 days to grow, but here we speed it up about 4 times so you can harvest in 7 days.

recycling.title: Recycling
recycling.body: The Space Station recycles about 98% of its water. Your breath and sweat become tomorrow's drinking water. Nothing is wasted.

exercise.title: Exercise
exercise.body: Astronauts on the Space Station train about 2 hours every day. Without exercise, bones and muscles get weak in space.

osdr_gym.title: Go to the gym!
osdr_gym.body: Mice lived on the Space Station for 37 days. Their leg bones got weaker, but their spines did not. Bones need work to stay strong. Go to the gym!

solar.title: Solar power
solar.body: NASA's polar design uses about 36 square meters of solar panels on a 10 meter mast to make about 10 kilowatts. That is what your four panel groups make.

dust.title: Dust
dust.body: Moon dust is sticky and sharp. When Apollo 11 lifted off, the dust it kicked up dimmed a sensor by 17% at once. Keep your panels clean.

packs.title: Power packs
packs.body: Your packs hold 120 kilowatt-hours each. A real pack that big would weigh about 800 kg. Swap packs so one charges while the other works.

cargo_landers.title: Cargo landers
cargo_landers.body: Real Moon outposts will bring most supplies from Earth. Here, robot landers drop rations and water, but they also kick up dust on your panels.

moonwalks.title: Moonwalks
moonwalks.body: The longest Moon walk was 7 hours 37 minutes, by Apollo 17 astronauts. Your suit meter shows the hours of oxygen you have left.

solar_storms.title: Solar storms
solar_storms.body: The Sun sends flares, called class M and X. The countdown you see is for the particles that arrive after the flash, not the light itself.

shelter_card.title: The shelter
shelter_card.body: About 80 centimeters of Moon soil can stop storm particles. Astronauts would hide in a buried shelter just like yours.

forecasts.title: Forecasts
forecasts.body: Scientists watch the Sun all day with satellites. When they see a flare, they warn astronauts so there is time to get safe.

moon_ice.title: Moon ice
moon_ice.body: Ice hides in craters that never see sunlight. NASA's LCROSS mission saw water mixed with other chemicals in a dark crater.

spacesuits.title: Spacesuits
spacesuits.body: A spacesuit holds about 8 hours of oxygen plus a 30-minute backup. Always watch your suit meter and head back in time.

silent_moon.title: Silent Moon
silent_moon.body: There is no air on the Moon, so sound cannot travel outside. Everything you hear on a mission comes through your suit.

ice_drink.title: Is moon ice drinkable?
ice_drink.body: Not yet! Moon ice has to be cleaned before anyone can drink it, and nobody has done that on the Moon. That is why we study samples.

gannon.title: The Gannon storm
gannon.body: In May 2024 the strongest geomagnetic storm since 2003 hit Earth. The Sun fired many flares in just a few days. The storm in this game is based on it.

feeding_person.title: Feeding a person
feeding_person.body: About 10 square meters of plants could feed one person. Radishes are a fresh extra, not a full meal plan.

csa_radish.title: Fresh food
csa_radish.body: Fresh food helps keep astronauts healthy. Canada's space agency studies how to grow food on the Moon, and the same ideas help people in remote places on Earth.
csa_radish.source: Canadian Space Agency, Food production on the Moon toolkit

shadows.title: Shadows at the pole
shadows.body: Near the equator the Moon's night lasts about 14 days. On a tall mast at the pole, shadows last only a few days. Charge both packs.

power_dark.title: Power in the dark
power_dark.body: NASA plans a 40 kilowatt fission reactor for future Moon bases, so they can have power even when the Sun is hidden.

radiation.title: Radiation on the surface
radiation.body: On the Moon's surface astronauts get about 1.37 millisieverts a day, like having an X-ray every day.

busy_sun.title: A busy Sun
busy_sun.body: NASA counted 82 notable flares in just one week of May 2024. The Sun was very busy.

radlab_storm.title: Radiation on the Station
radlab_storm.body: Detectors inside the Space Station measure radiation every day. One solar storm in September 2017 added about a quarter of a day's dose, even behind the walls.
radlab_storm.source: ISS dosimetry: DOSIS 3D-DOSTEL, via NASA OSDR RadLab

muscles.title: Muscles on the Moon
muscles.body: Scientists do not know yet how one sixth gravity changes bones over weeks. Maybe you will be the one to find out.

space_food.title: Space food
space_food.body: An astronaut eats about 2,500 to 2,800 calories a day. That is about 1.8 kg of food.

getting_braver.title: Getting braver
getting_braver.body: Apollo moonwalks grew from about 2.5 hours on Apollo 11 to about 7.5 hours on Apollo 17.

biggest_storms.title: The biggest storms
biggest_storms.body: The largest geomagnetic storm was in 1859. In August 1972 a storm hit between Apollo 16 and 17, and could have been deadly on the Moon.

why_forecasts_work.title: Why forecasts work
why_forecasts_work.body: Storm clouds from the Sun usually take 2 to 3 days to reach us. The fastest ever took 14.6 hours. That gives time to prepare.

potatoes.title: Potatoes in space
potatoes.body: On Space Shuttle mission STS-73, potato cuttings grew tiny potatoes in 16 days. Space farming started small.
